newsitem.title: UK: European physical copper still slow, scrap tight.
newsitem.headline: European physical copper still slow, scrap tight.

text.p: Spot demand for copper in Europe is still slow overall, although offtake of standard material has improved because of tightness in the scrap market, physical traders, merchants and producers said.

Fabricating plants are starting to increase production after the seasonal summer slowdown, but many are feeding off stocks or existing supply contracts rather than sourcing material from the spot market, they added.
"Business is pretty dead. There is not a great deal going on," said one European merchant.
"This time of year people always anticipate a bit of a bounce back in offtake. But there is no particular sign of it yet," a physical trader in London added.
Analysts said the sluggish conditions in early September should not be a surprise.
"Every year people say they expect an upturn in September. But while consumption tends to pick up, business doesn't because people work off stocks," said one.
"It is in the last two to three months that things tend to get going," he added.
Scrap supply is still limited, with traders and merchants sitting on material priced at higher levels before the price collapse in May and June.
"We are not seeing too much scrap come out at the moment. People are sitting on material priced at higher numbers and will probably continue to do so," a trader said.
The main consumer of scrap, the brass industry, is therefore having to purchase Russian material to cover against this.

"Blister copper has tightened and Russian copper sales are going well even though there is a lot of the material coming through," said a merchant. This helped lift Russian off-grade copper discounts in Rotterdam. They were quoted trading between $50 and $70 a tonne below LME cash values, up from $70 to $90 below in early August and $90 to $110 below in late May.
One trader saw Russian copper offered as high as $40 below.
Some industry sources said if good scrap continues to be held off market, it may have an impact on the overall supply/demand balance for copper this year.
"Instead of a small surplus this year we could get a small deficit if a lot of scrap is withheld," said a producer source.
But for LME deliverable material conditions are still slow in most major consuming countries in the region, traders said.
German offtake was sluggish despite early signs that the economy may be recovering.
"I would expect it to take another three to six months until the better economic climate starts to filter through to the copper market," the European merchant said.
"There is a lack of interest in the French market where inventories are good and new orders are lower than people expected, and Italy is not running at full steam yet," he added.
Traders said easing nearby spreads on the London Metal Exchange (LME) may help business, although renewed volatility in September is likely to have the opposite effect.
Except for Russian copper, most other copper differentials were unchanged from early August levels, reflecting the generally weak picture, traders said.
